explanation_text: Fishing boats on Wanwei Island park in numbered berths, and the position of a berth determines where each boat belongs, just like the position of a digit determines its value. A '1' in the tens place means ten, but in the hundreds place it means a hundred.
image_prompt: Illustrate a row of fishing boats docked in numbered berths on Wanwei Island beach, with the digits labeled as ones, tens, and hundreds to show how position changes value.

explanation_text: When a fisherman tosses more fish into a basket on the dock, the total grows; when some are sold or carried off, the total shrinks. That is exactly how addition and subtraction change an amount.
image_prompt: Show bamboo baskets of freshly caught fish being filled up and emptied out on a Guangxi fishing dock, with totals changing as fish are added or removed.

explanation_text: Setting out equal rows of jili fish traps in the tidal flats shows multiplication—a quick way to count repeated groups. Splitting the evening catch evenly among the boats shows division.
image_prompt: Display rows of identical jili fish traps arranged evenly across the tidal flats, showing equal grouping for multiplication and even sharing for division.

jing_culture: Pairs of oars on fishing boats
explanation_text: Fishing boats are rowed with oars in pairs; every boat uses two oars, so the oars line up in even numbers. If one oar is left over and no partner, that leftover represents an odd number.
image_prompt: Show fishing boats with their oars arranged in pairs on the beach, with one single oar standing alone to represent an odd number.

explanation_text: The colored floats strung along a fishing net repeat in rhythmic color sequences—blue, red, blue, red—just like skip counting repeats every 2, 5, or 10 in a number pattern.
image_prompt: Show a fishing net with repeating colored floats, highlighting every 5th float to illustrate skip counting by fives.

explanation_text: Comparing the piles of fish in two baskets shows which boat had a greater or smaller catch—the same way we compare numbers with greater than and less than.
image_prompt: Show several fish baskets with different amounts of seafood, using > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: A fisher may quickly guess that today's catch is 'about 80 kilograms' without weighing every fish. Estimating to a convenient rounded amount is exactly how rounding works.
image_prompt: Show a fisherman estimating a pile of fish by eye on the dock, with rounded weight labels such as 'about 80 kg' marked alongside.

explanation_text: When a boat's catch is shared equally among several families at the Three Saints' Temple fair, each family receives a fraction of the total catch.
image_prompt: Show a pile of fish being divided into equal shares among several families, each share labeled as a fraction of the whole catch.

jing_culture: Cutting a fish into equal parts
explanation_text: Cutting one fish into 2 equal halves or into 4 equal quarters still gives the very same fish—different fractions describing one equal amount, like equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show a fish cut first into halves, then into quarters, demonstrating equal portions that represent the same whole.

explanation_text: If several small catches combine into one larger pile, you describe the whole catch more simply—just as you reduce a fraction to its lowest terms.
image_prompt: Depict smaller piles of fish merging into one larger pile, with the fraction labels reduced to simplest form.

explanation_text: If a fisherman has 3 full baskets of shrimp and half a basket more, that is 3½—exactly the form of a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three full baskets and one half-full basket of shrimp labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When live fish fill more than one holding tank but are counted in equal tankfuls, the amount is greater than one whole—an improper fraction.
image_prompt: Show several holding tanks filled past one full portion, symbolizing fractions greater than 1.

explanation_text: Pouring portions of shrimp sauce from different jars into one big jar shows how fractional amounts add together to make a larger total.
image_prompt: Show smaller jars of shrimp sauce being poured together into one larger jar to make a total.

jing_culture: Scooping out part of a bucket
explanation_text: Scooping part of the fish water out of a bucket leaves a fractional part behind—this shows subtraction of a fraction from a whole.
image_prompt: Show a bucket of water on a fishing boat with part being scooped out, the remainder labeled as the fraction left.

explanation_text: If each family gets half of a half-share of fish, you are taking a fraction of a fraction—exactly what multiplying fractions means.
image_prompt: Show a plate of fish divided into halves, and one half divided again to show smaller portions.

explanation_text: If one netful of fish is divided evenly into smaller shares, you are finding how many smaller portions fit into the whole—like dividing a fraction by a fraction.
image_prompt: Show a netful of fish being split into smaller even shares to illustrate fractional division.

explanation_text: Weighing fish at the Fangchenggang market in kilograms and grams introduces decimals, like 1.5 kilograms meaning one and a half kilograms.
image_prompt: Show a market scale weighing a fish marked at 1.5 kg, with labels for 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 kilograms.

explanation_text: Whether a seller says 'half a kilogram' or '0.5 kilograms', both describe the same amount of fish—just like converting between fractions and decimals.
image_prompt: Show two labeled baskets, one marked ½ kg and another 0.5 kg, holding the same amount of fish.

explanation_text: When a student on Wanwei Island scores 90 out of 100 on a Vietnamese language test, that is 90%—a way to express parts per hundred.
image_prompt: Show a test paper with 90/100 written and a 90% mark beside it.

explanation_text: A 10% discount on a basket of oysters at the market shows how percents are used to find a part of a total number.
image_prompt: Show a market stall sign with oysters marked 'giảm 10%' (10% off) and price tags with reduced amounts.

explanation_text: If some baskets of fish arrive without a label, each represents an unknown weight—just like a variable in math stands for an unknown number.
image_prompt: Show labeled fish baskets (2 kg, 3 kg) and one unlabeled basket marked as x.

explanation_text: If you have 2 known baskets of shrimp and x more unknown ones on the boat, that is like writing the expression 2 + x.
image_prompt: Show two shrimp baskets plus one unlabeled basket, symbolized as 2 + x.

explanation_text: When two sides of a bamboo carry-pole hold equal weight, the pole balances level—just like both sides of an equation are equal.
image_prompt: Show a bamboo carry-pole balanced with equal loads on both sides, labeled as an equation.

explanation_text: If one side of a boat sits low because it is heavier, you fix the balance by adding or removing weight in one move—like solving a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a small fishing boat balanced level, with weights adjusted on one side to illustrate solving one-step equations.

explanation_text: Making fish sauce requires salting the fish first, then leaving it to ferment—two steps in the right order, just like solving a two-step equation.
image_prompt: Show the step sequence: salt the fish, then ferment in jars, then get the sauce, symbolizing step-by-step solving.

explanation_text: When one boat's catch is larger than another's, it shows inequality—the same idea as greater than or less than in math.
image_prompt: Show two piles of fish of different sizes with > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: Before steaming a fish you must first clean it and season it—the order matters. Math has its own required order of operations, like parentheses before exponents.
image_prompt: Show a cooking sequence for steamed fish where steps must happen in order, labeled like parentheses, exponents, etc.

explanation_text: If a broken oar is replaced with another of the same size, the boat rows the same—this is like substituting a value for a variable in an expression.
image_prompt: Show a missing oar being replaced with an identical one, representing substitution.

jing_culture: Boat lights on the sea at night
explanation_text: Each fishing boat light glowing on the night sea marks a single position—just like a point in geometry marks a location.
image_prompt: Show a night seascape with individual boat lights labeled as points on a coordinate grid.

jing_culture: Fishing lines dropped from a boat
explanation_text: Fishing lines lowered straight into the water stretch away from the boat and can extend forever in both directions, like geometric lines.
image_prompt: Show straight fishing lines extending down from a bamboo boat into the sea, representing geometric lines.

jing_culture: The spread of a cast net
explanation_text: When a fisherman casts his round net, the net opens into a spread that forms an angle at the caster's hands.
image_prompt: Show a fisherman casting a round net, with the opening angle clearly marked between the two edges.

explanation_text: The bamboo poles of a jili fish-trap frame cross at perfect right angles, making the trap strong and square—like perpendicular lines.
image_prompt: Show the bamboo frame of a fish trap with poles meeting at 90° angles.

explanation_text: The twin wakes trailing behind a rowed boat spread side by side and never meet—exactly like parallel lines.
image_prompt: Show two straight boat wakes running side by side across the water behind a small fishing boat.

jing_culture: Fishing nets laid flat to dry
explanation_text: Laid flat to dry on the beach, the frames and mesh of different nets form closed geometric shapes with straight edges—polygons.
image_prompt: Show fishing nets spread flat on the beach forming various closed geometric shapes.

explanation_text: The small sails raised on Jing bamboo boats are cut in triangles, giving them three straight sides and three corners.
image_prompt: Show triangular sails on bamboo fishing boats near the Guangxi coast.

explanation_text: The openings woven into fishing nets form four-sided shapes—squares and rectangles that repeat across the whole net.
image_prompt: Show a close view of woven fishing net mesh with repeating square and rectangular openings.

jing_culture: Walking the edge of a fish corral
explanation_text: Measuring the distance all the way around the outside of a fish corral is like finding the perimeter of a shape.
image_prompt: Show people walking around the outside edge of a round jili fish corral with a dashed perimeter line.

jing_culture: Drying nets spread on the beach
explanation_text: The amount of beach covered by a drying net spread flat represents its area—the space inside its outline.
image_prompt: Show a fishing net spread on the beach, shaded to show the area it covers.

explanation_text: The amount of seawater a holding tank can carry for live fish represents its volume.
image_prompt: Show holding tanks filled to different levels to illustrate volume.

explanation_text: The round jili fish corral and the round soundboard of the duxianqin monochord are perfect circles, illustrating radius, diameter, and circumference.
image_prompt: Show a round jili fish trap seen from above, labeled with radius and diameter lines.

explanation_text: No matter the size of the round resonator of a duxianqin, its circumference divided by its diameter is always the same constant—π.
image_prompt: Show a circular duxianqin resonator labeled with circumference and diameter measurements.

explanation_text: Oyster racks arranged in tidy rows and columns across the tidal flats resemble a coordinate grid, where each rack has its own position.
image_prompt: Show an aerial view of oyster racks in rows and columns, labeled with x and y coordinates.

jing_culture: Marking boat positions on a sea chart
explanation_text: Marking each fishing boat's position on a sea chart is like plotting points on a coordinate plane.
image_prompt: Show a sea chart of the waters around the three Jing islands with boat positions marked as points.

explanation_text: The woven patterns of Jing fishing nets and the decorations at the Ha festival mirror each other across a center line, showing symmetry.
image_prompt: Show a symmetrical fishing net pattern split by a mirror line.

explanation_text: When boats turn, shift position, or mirror their course during a day of fishing, they move through geometric transformations.
image_prompt: Show fishing boats turning and shifting positions on the water to illustrate transformations.

explanation_text: When making shrimp sauce, the balance of shrimp to salt represents a ratio, like 3 parts shrimp to 1 part salt.
image_prompt: Show a shrimp sauce jar labeled with shrimp and salt ratios, like 3:1.

explanation_text: When a fisherman scales up a small net pattern to weave a larger one while keeping the mesh identical, that is maintaining proportion.
image_prompt: Show a small and a large fishing net with the same proportions.

explanation_text: The number of fish a boat catches in one hour of fishing is a unit rate.
image_prompt: Show a fishing boat with its catch measured as fish caught per hour.

explanation_text: Drawing a small map of the three Jing islands while keeping real distances proportional is a scale drawing.
image_prompt: Show the three islands and a smaller scaled map beside them with a scale legend.

explanation_text: If a boat's daily catch grows from 100 to 120 kilograms, that is a 20% increase—an example of percent change.
image_prompt: Show a pile of fish growing in size with a +20% label.

explanation_text: Writing down how many kilograms of fish, shrimp, and oysters each boat brings in every day is an example of data collection.
image_prompt: Show a fisherman marking tallies of the daily catch on a clipboard at the dock.

explanation_text: Using a graph to show how much fish was caught in each season helps visualize trends in the fishing year.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph comparing fish catches across the four seasons.

explanation_text: Finding the average number of fish a boat catches per day shows the mean of all its daily catches.
image_prompt: Show a table of daily catches with the average value highlighted.

explanation_text: When the daily catches of all the boats are arranged from smallest to largest, the catch in the middle is the median.
image_prompt: Show baskets of catches lined up in order with the middle one highlighted as the median.

explanation_text: If most of the fish brought in on a given day are anchovies, then anchovy is the mode of that day's catch.
image_prompt: Show different kinds of fish with one type being clearly the most common.

explanation_text: The gap between the biggest and smallest catch among the boats shows the range of the data.
image_prompt: Show a bar chart with the shortest and tallest bars marked for the range.

explanation_text: Each bar in the graph represents the catch of one boat, making quick comparisons easy.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph labeled by boat names with their daily catch totals.

explanation_text: A line graph shows how the size of the catch changes from month to month across the fishing year.
image_prompt: Show a line graph labeled with months and fish catch amounts.

explanation_text: A pie chart can show the share of fish, shrimp, oysters, and crabs in a boat's total catch.
image_prompt: Show a pie chart divided into seafood categories with percentages.

explanation_text: Before setting out, a fisherman may guess how likely it is that the day's catch will be good—that likelihood is probability.
image_prompt: Show boats heading out at dawn with probability labels above each one showing the chance of a good catch.

explanation_text: The repeated wave-and-fish motifs on Jing nets and Ha festival banners represent visual patterns that repeat in sequence.
image_prompt: Show repeating wave and fish designs in traditional Jing craft.

explanation_text: If each speed of a boat gives one specific distance traveled per hour, it is like a function—each input gives exactly one output.
image_prompt: Show a graph linking boat speed (input) to distance traveled (output).
